chapter_theme: First songs at Viralimalai (விராலிமலை, 1 of 2): the poet confesses bondage to courtesans who sell their bodies, to his own flattery of misers and his poems on women, and to the malas, and asks for the feet, for samadhi and for the teaching of jnana beyond the tattvas; the praise names Vayalur, where Murugan commanded the poet to sing, and identifies him with Tamil saints.
structure_note: Courtesan and body songs (569, 574, 576, 578, 580, 582), the long head-to-foot song 572; songs of yoga and knowledge (570, 573, 575, 581); begging from patrons (571, 579); a song of meditation on Murugan's form (568); and 577, a string of Siva's names.

568.reading: The poet asks that, lowly as he is, he may every day hold in thought Murugan's flower faces crowned with gem garlands, his twelve arms, his two fragrant feet, Valli and Indra's daughter on either side, the vel, the peacock and his beautiful form of true knowledge. The praise tells how at Madurai, when the forty-nine poets disputed the meaning of a work, Murugan came as a mute merchant's child at Alavai and settled it, and names him nephew of Krishna who hid the sun with his discus, at Viralimalai by the Kaveri.
568.nuance: The plea is a meditation list (தியானம்), the god's form part by part, rather than a confession. ஏழேழு பேர்கள் கூற வரு பொருள் அதிகாரம் ... ஊமர் போல வணிகரில் ஊடாடி: the Madurai story of the mute child who judged the commentaries on Iraiyanar's Akapporul, here told of Murugan, so he is identified with a figure of the Tamil Sangam. பாநு மறைவுசெய் is Krishna covering the sun in the Bharata war.

569.reading: The poet calls himself the one who sang poems of every kind, from feet to hair, on women who put a price on breasts like Meru and stir desire with words of milk, syrup and honey; a goblin-witted, ungenerous, untrue sinner without penance, a fool busy with bondage, he asks to become the dust of Murugan's feet and not fall into hell. The praise shows Death and his messengers afraid, Brahma and Vishnu fleeing, Vedic priests chanting Sivaya nama as Sura dies, and the groves of Viralimalai where bees hum ragas.
569.nuance: பாதாதி கேசமாக வகைவகை கவிபாடும்: the poet confesses not only desire but misuse of his art, poems describing women from foot to head, a recognised genre. பசுபாச வ்யாபார மூடன் uses the Siddhanta terms for the bound soul and its bond. முலையினை விலைகூறி names the sale.

570.reading: The poet asks Murugan to think of him so that ascetics who speak no idle word may say of him day and night that he has no passion, no diversion, no greed and no infatuation, and so that he gains the experience of samadhi in which the mind dissolves into the transcendent that pervades all moving and unmoving worlds. The praise names Siva who wears the moon and the river and crushed Ravana's arms, and Murugan the bridegroom of the hunters' daughter, at Siramalai, Piranmalai and Viralimalai.
570.nuance: மநோலய சமாதி அநுபூதி: samadhi as the dissolution of mind, a yogic term. The long run of Sanskrit epithets (சதாசிவ மயேசுர சகலலோக சராசர வியாபக பராபர) may describe the state sought or the god addressed, and உமாபுருஷன் என may compare the poet to Siva or be divided otherwise.

571.reading: The poet asks whether, not fixing his mind on the stainless, ancient, transcendent one whom Siva, Vishnu and Brahma praise and who is the form of heaven, earth and all beings, he will go with longing for gifts to faithless, indifferent men of empty fame. The praise plays on Ravana's name in telling of Rama, names Murugan the younger brother of the elephant-faced lord of arts, and ends at Viralimalai.
571.nuance: The second line of the plea (துரால்புகழ் பராதின கராவுள பராமுக துரோகரை தராசையுற்று அடைவேனோ) seems to name patrons, men of chaff-like fame who turn their faces away, as in 579 and 589. The song is a dense chain of Sanskrit compounds and its division is doubtful throughout.

572.reading: In a long rhythm the poet describes a woman from her bathed and scented hair to her anklets, and asks whether a day will come when, no longer melting in such women's wiles, the delusion ends, grace comes into his hands, and he sees the high way of devotion and the path to supreme liberation. The praise is a long battle in drum syllables, with sun and moon restored and the gods regaining their rule, and recalls that at Vayalur Murugan appeared before the poet and told him to sing the rare great Thiruppugazh so that his delusion and impurity might end; it ends at Viralimalai with Murugan on the peacock.
572.nuance: வயலியில் ... மயலொடு மலமற அரிய பெரிய திருப்புகழ் விளம்பு என் முன் அற்புதம் எழுந்தருள் குக: an autobiographical line, the poet's own call at Vayalur to sing the book, set inside the praise. The woman's description is a full head-to-foot catalogue of the kind 569 confesses to having composed.

573.reading: The poet asks whether the knowledge handed on by gurus, one after another, who teach japa until the mantra takes form, a crore of fire-offerings, devotion to the Agamas, holding the one syllable and restraining the breath, can be a refuge; if Siva the fire-dancer himself gave the light and the attainment of knowledge, that would be it, and he has not found it. The praise tells of the Kauravas destroyed and Kunti's sons ruling by justice, Vishnu the dwarf who grew tall, and names Murugan Siva's son with the vel at Viralimalai, the master who cured the Pandya king's fever and straightened his hump at Madurai.
573.nuance: The plea weighs ritual and yogic discipline taught by human gurus (ஜெபித்து, ஓம சித்தி, ஆகமத்து, ஊதை) against knowledge given by Siva and asks whether the first is a refuge (தஞ்சமாமோ). மாறன் வெப்பு வளைகூனையே நிமிர்த்த: Sambandar's cure of the Pandya, so Murugan is again Sambandar. The split of தரியாத போதகத்தர் is uncertain, and so whether these gurus are praised or doubted.

574.reading: The poet describes women who bind men with desire and show them a pit to stumble into, and in deliberately foul images, a well drawn by bucket, a channel of old stains, a rotting hole stopped with cloth where streams flow, calls their sex a ruined mire, and asks Murugan to take him as his own so that he does not sink in it. The praise tells of the Bharata war, Vidura, Drona, Jayadratha and Arjuna, Krishna as Dharma's envoy and Arjuna's charioteer as Murugan's uncle, at Viralimalai with Uma at Siva's half.
574.nuance: அளறில் அழுந்தாமல்: அளறு is mire and also hell, the word the Kural uses for the courtesan. The method is that of the Naladiyar's body chapters, desire countered by naming the body's filth. The images are crude and partly obscure (இறைவைகொளுங் கூவல், சீலை தீற்று), and the last two lines of the praise nearly repeat each other.

575.reading: The poet defines Sivayoga as the abiding of everything, the five elements, six religions, mantras, Vedas, Puranas and arts, the fifty-one letters, all beings, Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, sun and moon, the ajapa, bindu and nada, as one form, its own nature, and asks whether, with the malas of anava, maya and karma gone, he will gain that path in the line of the teaching guru. The praise shows the demons routed, the gods back in Indra's world, the goddess crying 'Hara Hara Sankara' as the vel pierces Meru, and ash-smeared sages in samadhi in the caves of Viralimalai where peacocks dance.
575.nuance: ஏக வடிவம் அதன் சொரூபமதாக உறைவது சிவயோகம்: Sivayoga as seeing all things abiding as one form, which is pervasion turned into a practice. The three malas are named exactly (ஆணவ மாயை கருமம்), and the path is to be had in a guru's tradition (உபதேச குருபர சம்ப்ரதாயமொடு).

576.reading: The poet describes lovemaking in detail and asks whether, before his youth turns to age, he will come to know and gain Murugan's feet. The praise tells of Rama's army of bears and monkeys, Lanka shaken and Ravana's ten heads falling like palm fruit, Krishna who kicked down the marudu trees, and asks Murugan at Viralimalai to take the poet, the son who worships him gladly as Kanda, into hereditary loving service.
576.nuance: இளமை கிழம்படு முன்: the urgency is time, to reach the feet before youth becomes age. வழிவழி அன்புசெய் தொண்டு: servitude by succession, the வழியடிமை of other songs.

577.reading: The first half is a chain of Siva's names, the elephant's foe, Tripura's foe, Kama's foe, the dancer in fire, lord of Kailasa, skull-bearer, great yogi, wearer of matted hair, the knower beyond words, rider of the bull, dancer in the forest, ending with a plea for grace and the city of supreme knowledge. The praise shows Brahma fleeing, Meru whirling, Sura dying, the world-rim hill tilting and vultures and ghouls dancing on the battlefield, and names Murugan the Meru of compassion at Viraliyur.
577.nuance: The plea is almost wholly epithets of Siva (கரிபுராரி காமாரி திரிபுராரி தீயாடி ... பசுவேறி), as if Murugan were addressed as Siva himself, or Siva first praised and then asked. Which is meant, and what பரம ஞான வூர்பூத asks for, is unclear.

578.reading: The poet describes women's eyes as Kama's weapons that carry off young men's lives, running to the earrings, sharp as sword and spear at the corners, Yama's messengers, rivals of the blue lily, and says that because Murugan once appeared and saved his servant from the delusion that wears endless blame, he will never forget his power. The praise names the goddess in her many forms and the six Krittika mothers who reared Kumara, and Murugan who taught the true meaning of the Upanishads and Vedas to Siva of Kailasa, at Viralimalai where Siva worship and giving never fail.
578.nuance: Unusually the song gives thanks rather than asking: நீ தோற்றி முன் நாளும் அடிமையை ஈடேற்றுதலால் உன் வலிமையை மறவேனே, a past rescue remembered, perhaps the same as the Vayalur call in 572. வேலின் முனை கடை யமதூதர்: the eye is Death's servant, a classical figure. The teaching of Siva is of Upanishad and Veda meaning, not explicitly Om.

579.reading: The poet confesses praising the man who never gives as if he were Kubera, fawning and wandering in vain, bearing burdens, wasted by poverty, without seeking Murugan's grace to end it, and his heart deluded by women's breasts; he asks whether, before his worthless body and life ache and die, Murugan's tongue will say 'Death, do not touch him'. The praise names Murugan son of the mother who bore the seven worlds, the lord of knowledge born where the bindu meets the root whorl, at Viralimalai of rain-fed groves and flowering pools.
579.nuance: கொடாதவனையே புகழ்ந்து குபேரனெனவே மொழிந்து: the poet's begging songs to misers, a confession of the court poet's trade. தொடாய் மறலியே நீ: the plea at death is for a single spoken word from Murugan to Death. நடாதசுழி மூல விந்து names the kundalini centre in the praise.

580.reading: The poet lists the courtesans' arts in a string of names: wholly of maya, endless schemers, eyes that saw through lives, who melt even sages with laughter, who cry 'come, come', rouse desire, quarrel when not paid, drink themselves wild, and steal without counting sin, and asks whether a bond with these women of low conduct who sell their breasts is fitting. The praise tells of the child Krishna drinking the cowherd women's milk, curd and ghee, tied to the mortar and beaten by Yasoda until he cried, whose flute calls back the herds, as uncle of Murugan of Vayalur, at Viralimalai.
580.nuance: ஈயாத போதில் அறப் பிணக்கிகள் and விலைத் தனத்தியர்: money is named twice. The list form (each name ending -கள், -கிகள்) is a set piece of abuse. The Krishna story is told with unusual tenderness, his ears held as he weeps.

581.reading: The poet says that though he is a great sinner walking maya's twisted way, with infatuation, desire and anger unceasing, Murugan is now his mother and father; he has not studied the four Vedas or the Agamas, so that his days not pass in vain he asks for the teaching of knowledge beyond the thirty-six. The praise names the child adorned with fragrant sandal, Murugan of Vayalur and Viralimalai, the six-faced son of the lord of ghouls and goblins, foe of Sura, lord of the gods.
581.nuance: ஆறாறு மீதில் ஞானோபதேசம்: teaching beyond the six times six, the thirty-six tattvas of Saiva doctrine. The poet's lack of learning (நான் ஓதினேனும் இலை) is made the ground of the plea, not a bar to it.

582.reading: The poet describes lovemaking, hair loosened, girdle slipping, eyes closing, cries like peacock, quail and cuckoo, and says that even if he sleeps exhausted on the breasts after union he will not forget Murugan's lotus feet. The praise names Murugan dwelling on the hill of Viralimalai with drums sounding, worshipped by the three worlds and praised by the goddess who once felled Meru with an arrow, who killed Sura with the vel, freed the gods from prison and resettled the worlds.
582.nuance: துயில் கூரினும் அம்புயதாள் துணை மறவேனே: the song does not ask to leave the embrace but vows remembrance of the feet within it. It may be read as hyperbole of devotion or as a different stance from songs that ask to be freed from women.

links.note: Both call the courtesan's body a mire (அளறு) into which men sink; the Kural's word also means hell, and 574 asks to be taken by the Lord so as not to sink there.

Both counter desire by naming the body's openings and their seepage: the Naladiyar's pot oozing filth from nine holes, 574's rotting, cloth-stopped hole. The Naladiyar calls the lover a fool; 574 asks for rescue.
Both make the woman's eye Death: the Kural's lover cannot tell if her look is Death, an eye or a doe, while 578 calls the eye-corners Yama's messengers in a confession it was saved from.

Both say rites and recitation do not yield the truth: Tirumular's men perform many rites and recite hymns yet wither without understanding; 573 doubts that japa, fire-offerings and Agamic learning passed down by gurus can be a refuge without Siva's own gift.

Both define Sivayoga. Tirumular makes it knowing the conscient and non-conscient and becoming one's own light; 575 makes it seeing every element, scripture, letter and god abide as one form, and adds that the malas must go first.

27 asks to see clearly how to leave the embrace and reach the feet; 582 vows to remember the feet even asleep on the breasts after union, so devotion is placed inside desire rather than after it, if the vow is not read as hyperbole.

The Thiruppugazh song asks to hold daily in thought (நாளு நினைவது) Murugan's form counted part by part: faces, twelve arms (ஈராறு தோளு), two feet, consorts, vel and peacock. The Tirumanthiram verse counts Sadasiva's five faces, fifteen eyes and ten hands and ends with that Lord entering and filling the heart (நெஞ்சு புகுந்து நிறைந்து). Both use the counted iconic form as the content of meditation, for different gods.

Both songs confess the same misuse of the poet's art: 569 calls himself the one who sang poems of every kind from foot to hair (பாதாதி கேசமாக வகைவகை கவிபாடும்) on women who price their breasts, and 1150 the poet who wandered singing women from foot to head (பாதாதி கேசம் அளவும் பாடும் கவிஞனாய்). Read together they show the head-to-foot description of women as a named genre the poet repents of, in both cases alongside the term பசு பாசம.

569 confesses having sung women from foot to hair (பாதாதி கேசமாக ... கவிபாடும்). 572, in the same set of Viralimalai songs, is itself such a catalogue, from bathed hair (குந்தளமும்) to anklets (பரிபுர ... பதமும்), turned at the end into a plea that the delusion end. The pairing shows the poet using the confessed genre inside the devotional song.

The Thiruppugazh song asks for the experience of samadhi in which the mind dissolves (மநோலய சமாதி அநுபூதி). The Tirumanthiram verse describes the samadhi in which the mind melts and becomes Siva (சித்தம் உருக்கிச் சிவமாம் சமாதி) and whose bliss does not leave. Both define samadhi by the dissolving of mind, one as a request, the other as a report of its fruit.

571 asks whether, not fixing his mind on the transcendent, he will go with longing for gifts (தராசையுற்று அடைவேனோ) to faithless, averted men of chaff-like fame (துரால்புகழ் ... பராமுக துரோகரை). 306 asks not to perish in vain like bards who seek out the wealth of deceitful misers and call them Pari and Kari. Both set the court poet's begging against praise of Murugan; 306 makes plain the bardic trade that 571's dense compounds name.

572 recalls in its praise that at Vayalur Murugan appeared before the poet and told him to sing the rare great Thiruppugazh so that delusion and mala might end (வயலியில் ... அரிய பெரிய திருப்புகழ் விளம்பு). The second song of the book likewise names the grace that told him to sing Thiruppugazh (திருப்புகழ் ... செப்பென எனக்கருள்கை), at Seyppathi, usually taken as Vayalur. The two are the book's own accounts of its commission; 572 adds its purpose, the ending of மயல் and மலம்.

575 asks to gain the path of Sivayoga in the line of the teaching guru (உபதேச குருபர சம்ப்ரதாயமொடு ஏயும் நெறி). 573 asks whether knowledge handed on by gurus one after another, with japa, fire offerings and breath restraint, can be a refuge (தஞ்சமாமோ), and says it would be so only if Siva gave it (தழலாடி ... ஞான சித்தி தருமாகில்). Read together, 573 puts a condition on the guru-lineage 575 trusts: the teaching avails when the Lord gives it; this depends on the uncertain reading of தரியாத போதகத்தர்.

The Thiruppugazh song asks whether, before youth turns to age (இளமை கிழம்படு முன்), he will come to know and gain the feet. The Tirumanthiram verse says youth wears away and is gone, so hold to Nandi while life is still in you (உயிருள்ள போதே). Both make the passing of youth the reason for turning to the Lord now; the song asks it from inside the pleasures it describes.

576 asks to reach the feet before youth becomes age. The Naladiyar verse pictures the man who fails to: speech failing, leaning on a staff, teeth gone, still with eyes set on desire in the house, with no path to safety (ஏம நெறிபடருமாறு இல்லையே). The Naladiyar shows the end the song's urgency is meant to avoid: desire outliving youth with no way out.

Among its names for courtesans the Thiruppugazh song calls them women who quarrel bitterly when not given (ஈயாத போதில் அறப் பிணக்கிகள்) and who sell their breasts (விலைத் தனத்தியர்). The Naladiyar verse says their love, like a lamp's light when the oil is gone, ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Both make payment the condition of the courtesan's affection, and the song asks on that ground whether a bond (உறவு) with them is fitting.

The Thiruppugazh song, its singer unlearned in Vedas and Agamas, asks for the teaching of knowledge beyond the six sixes (ஆறாறு மீதில் ஞானோபதேசம்). The Tirumanthiram verse reports that to one who did not know the nature of the six sixes (ஆறாறின் தன்மை அறியாது இருந்தேனுக்கு) Nandi made it known and stood beyond them. The same term, ஆறாறு, gives the request in one and its fulfilment through the guru in the other.

source_issues: Song 568: one corrupt character in லு஡டாடி (line 17), probably லூடாடி.
Song 571: unflagged garble செர்ருபமி (line 6), probably ஸ்வரூப; the same garble appears as செர்ருப in 580 and 584.
Song 573: one corrupt character in னு஡றில் (line 12), probably ஊறில்.
Song 574: one corrupt character in லு஡த்தை (line 5), probably ஊத்தை; the last two lines of the song nearly repeat lines 13 and 14.
Song 575: two corrupt characters, புண்ட஡ணகன் (line 5, புண்டரீகன்) and வயலு஡ரா (line 18, வயலூரா).
Song 580: three corrupt characters, வா஡ண ரி஡ணர் (line 6, வாரீர் வாரீர்) and வயலு஡ரா (line 21); also the unflagged செர்ருப (line 1).
Song 581: one corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 12); also the unflagged ச்முக (line 13), probably ஷண்முக.
